n: The Bible opens not with a battle between gods, as Babylonian myths did, but with one God speaking a world into order. 'Without form and void' (Latin inanis et vacua) describes chaos being tamed, not matter being fought. The 'Spirit of God moved over the waters' is read by Christians as the first glimpse of the Trinity at work.

t: 'Let us make man to our image'
n: The plural 'let us' puzzled readers for centuries: Jewish tradition heard God addressing his heavenly court, Christian readers heard the Trinity. 'Image and likeness' is the ground of human dignity in both faiths — every person, not only kings, bears the royal stamp of God.

God does not tire; the rest of the seventh day is a model. It founds the Sabbath, the first thing in Scripture called 'holy'. Christians later moved their weekly rest to Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, calling it 'the eighth day' — creation begun again.

'Knowledge of good and evil' means deciding for oneself what is good and evil — moral autonomy, not information. Every other tree is given freely; the single prohibition makes obedience possible and love real. Jerome's Latin morte morieris, 'thou shalt die the death', is a Hebrew intensifier: 'you will surely die'.

Christians call this verse the first promise of a redeemer: the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head. The Vulgate famously reads ipsa conteret, 'she shall crush', which shaped centuries of Marian art (the Virgin standing on a serpent). The Hebrew has 'he' — the offspring himself. Both readings point the same direction: victory over evil through a child of Eve.

Before expelling them, God himself makes clothes for the couple — judgment wrapped in care. The cherubim and flaming sword guard the way back to the tree of life; the Book of Revelation ends with that way reopened (Rev 22:14). The whole Bible is the story of the road back to Eden.

Cain's sneer is the first recorded lie to God's face. The answer of the whole Torah is yes. 'The voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me' introduces a theme that runs to the Letter to the Hebrews, where Christ's blood 'speaketh better than that of Abel' (Heb 12:24) — pleading mercy instead of vengeance.

t: The 'sons of God' and the giants
n: One of the strangest passages in Scripture. Early readers (and the Book of Enoch) took the 'sons of God' as fallen angels; later Jewish and Christian teachers read them as the godly line of Seth marrying into the line of Cain. The 'giants' (Hebrew Nephilim) belong to a world sliding into violence before the Flood.

t: Sacrifice and the promise of seasons
n: Noah's first act on dry land is worship. God's response — 'I will no more curse the earth... seedtime and harvest, cold and heat... shall not cease' — is the charter of a stable, trustworthy creation. The rainbow of the next chapter is a war-bow hung up in the sky, pointed away from the earth.

The tower is a ziggurat, a Mesopotamian temple-mountain; its builders want to 'make a name' for themselves. God's scattering is both judgment and mercy — limiting how far a united arrogance can go. Pentecost (Acts 2), where people of every tongue hear one message, is Babel reversed.

Three promises — land, descendants, and blessing for 'all the kindred of the earth' — govern everything that follows in the Bible. Abram is seventy-five, childless, and told to walk away from everything. Paul makes this the model of faith: he believed a promise he could not see (Rom 4).

A king of Salem (Jerusalem) appears from nowhere, brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram, and vanishes. Psalm 109 (110) and the Letter to the Hebrews make him a type of Christ — a priest not by descent but by God's word. The Roman Canon of the Mass still names 'thy high priest Melchisedech'.

Abram simply trusts, and God counts it as righteousness. This single verse became the hinge of the Reformation debate on faith and works. Paul cites it (Rom 4, Gal 3) to say the promise came before the Law; James cites it (Jas 2) to say faith proved itself in what Abraham did.

Ancient covenants were sealed by cutting animals in two and passing between the halves — 'may this be done to me if I break my word'. Here only God, as a smoking furnace and a lamp of fire, passes through. The covenant rests on God's oath alone; Abram is asleep.

Abraham sees three men and addresses them as one 'Lord'. Christian tradition saw here a foreshadowing of the Trinity — the subject of Rublev's famous icon. Hospitality to strangers becomes a sacred duty: 'some have entertained angels unawares' (Heb 13:2).

'Wilt thou destroy the just with the wicked?' Abraham haggles God down from fifty righteous to ten. The scene establishes that God's justice can be argued with in prayer, and that a few righteous people can shield a whole city — an idea Jesus echoes when he calls his disciples 'the salt of the earth'.

The hardest chapter in Genesis. God asks for the son on whom every promise depends; Abraham obeys without a word of complaint; Isaac carries the wood himself. Jews call it the Akedah and read it on the New Year; Christians see the Father who did not spare his own Son (Rom 8:32). 'God will provide' (Dominus videbit) names the mountain — later the site of the Temple.

t: A birthright for a bowl of lentils
n: Esau, famished, trades the rights of the firstborn for red stew. The story is told with contempt for his shrug: 'he ate, and drank, and went his way'. Hebrews 12:16 makes him the type of the person who sells the eternal for the immediate. Jacob's cunning is not praised either; both brothers will pay for this.

Alone and running from his brother, Jacob sleeps on a stone and sees a stairway with angels, God standing above it. 'This is no other but the house of God, and the gate of heaven' (Bethel means 'house of God'). Jesus applies the image to himself: the angels ascend and descend 'upon the Son of man' (John 1:51).

On the night before he must face Esau, Jacob wrestles a mysterious man until daybreak, is wounded in the hip, and refuses to let go without a blessing. He receives a new name, Israel, 'he who strives with God'. The nation is named after a limping man who would not let go of God.

The Hebrew describes a long-sleeved tunic — the dress of someone who does not do manual work. Jacob repeats the favouritism that wrecked his own family. The Joseph story (chapters 37–50) is the longest continuous narrative in Genesis and reads like a novel: betrayal, prison, power, and a forgiveness that saves the whole family.

Joseph reveals himself to the brothers who sold him and refuses to see it as their crime alone: 'not by your counsel was I sent hither, but by the will of God'. Genesis 50:20 will put it more sharply — 'you thought evil against me, but God turned it into good'. This is the Bible's first full statement of providence.

t: The lion of Juda and the sceptre
n: Jacob's deathbed blessing gives Judah the kingship: 'the sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda... till he come that is to be sent'. The Vulgate's donec veniat qui mittendus est was read as a prophecy of the Messiah, and Revelation 5:5 calls Christ 'the lion of the tribe of Juda'.

A bush burning without being consumed: the Fathers saw an image of God's presence that does not destroy what it fills, and of the Virgin who bore God without harm. 'Put off the shoes from thy feet' — the first 'holy ground' in the Bible is not a temple but a place where God speaks.

Asked his name, God answers Ego sum qui sum. The Hebrew YHWH — four consonants Jews do not pronounce, reading 'Adonai' (Lord) instead — is rendered Dominus in the Vulgate and 'the LORD' in most English Bibles. Jesus' 'before Abraham was made, I am' (John 8:58) claims this name.

A lamb without blemish, its blood on the doorposts, eaten in haste: the Pasch (Passover) becomes Israel's founding memory, kept every spring to this day. John's Gospel times the crucifixion to the slaughter of the lambs and calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God'; Paul says plainly, 'Christ our pasch is sacrificed' (1 Cor 5:7).

The crossing of the Red Sea (Hebrew 'Sea of Reeds') is the central act of salvation in the Old Testament, sung about in Psalms and prophets. Paul calls it a baptism (1 Cor 10:2); the Easter Vigil reads this chapter every year while the newly baptised wait at the font.

The name manna is the question the Israelites asked — man hu, 'what is it?' A daily bread that cannot be hoarded, it teaches trust one day at a time. Jesus sets himself against it: 'your fathers did eat manna and are dead... I am the living bread' (John 6).

Hebrew calls them the 'ten words', not commandments. Catholics and Lutherans number them one way (the prohibition of idols folded into the first; two commandments on coveting), Jews, Orthodox and Reformed another. The first tablet concerns God, the second one's neighbour — the two loves Jesus later names as the whole Law.

Moses reads the law, the people say 'we will do it', and he sprinkles them with blood: 'this is the blood of the covenant'. At the Last Supper Jesus uses exactly these words of the cup (Matt 26:28). The covenant at Sinai and the new covenant are meant to be heard together.

Forty days without Moses and the people build a god they can see. Aaron's excuse — 'I cast the gold into the fire, and there came out this calf' — is one of the Bible's dry jokes. The calf was probably meant as a throne or footstool for the invisible God; the sin was making God manageable.

Moses, God's friend, asks to see his glory and is allowed only to see him pass from behind. No one sees God and lives — until John writes, 'we saw his glory' (John 1:14). The cleft of the rock where Moses hid became, for the Fathers, the wounded side of Christ.

'The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, patient and of much compassion, and true' — this self-description is quoted more often inside the Old Testament than any other verse (Psalms, Joel, Jonah, Nehemiah). Mercy comes first and reaches 'thousands'; punishment 'to the third and fourth generation' — the household living under one roof.

Two goats: one sacrificed, one sent into the desert carrying the people's sins. Jerome's caper emissarius gave English its word 'scapegoat'. Yom Kippur is still the holiest day of the Jewish year; Hebrews 9 reads the whole ritual as a sketch of Christ entering heaven with his own blood.

Buried in a chapter of ritual and civil laws is the verse Jesus called the second greatest commandment. Leviticus goes on (19:34) to extend it to the stranger 'as one of the same country'. Rabbi Akiva called this verse 'the great principle of the Torah'.

Every fiftieth year debts are cancelled, slaves freed and land returned to its original families — a built-in reset against permanent poverty. The word comes from yobel, the ram's horn that announced it. Jesus opens his ministry by reading Isaiah 61 — 'to preach the acceptable year of the Lord' — the Jubilee proclaimed for good (Luke 4).

'The Lord bless thee and keep thee; the Lord show his face to thee...' — the oldest biblical text ever found, inscribed on silver amulets from about 600 BC. Its threefold form led Christians to hear the Trinity; it still closes services in synagogues and churches alike.

Bitten by fiery serpents, the people are healed by looking at a bronze serpent lifted on a pole — the cause of death becomes the sign of healing. Jesus makes it the first explanation of the cross: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up' (John 3:14).

A pagan prophet hired to curse Israel is rebuked by his own donkey, who sees the angel he cannot. The comedy is deliberate: the seer is blind, the beast sees. Balaam ends by blessing Israel instead and uttering the oracle of the star out of Jacob (24:17) — which the Magi were later thought to have followed.

'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord' — the creed Jews recite morning and evening and bind on arm and forehead (tefillin) and doorpost (mezuzah). Jesus quotes it as the first and greatest commandment (Mark 12:29). 'Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart' turns law into love.

Moses promises that God will raise up a prophet like himself. Israel waited for 'the Prophet' (see John 1:21, 6:14), and Peter in Acts 3:22 says that prophet is Jesus. Deuteronomy ends by noting no such prophet had yet appeared (34:10).

t: 'The word is very nigh unto thee'
n: The commandment is not in heaven or beyond the sea; it is 'in thy mouth and in thy heart'. Paul lifts this whole passage into Romans 10 and applies it to faith in Christ: the word you need is not far away.

Moses sees the promised land from Mount Nebo and dies without entering it, buried by God himself in a grave 'no man hath known'. Jewish tradition says he died 'by the kiss of God'. Moses' unfinished journey haunts the New Testament: he finally stands in the land at the Transfiguration (Matt 17).

A Canaanite prostitute hides Israel's spies and hangs a scarlet cord from her window. She is saved, joins Israel, and appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. Hebrews and James both hold her up as a model — of faith and of works respectively. The scarlet cord was read by the Fathers as the blood of Christ.

No siege engines, only priests, trumpets and a week of silent marching. The conquest is presented as God's act, with Israel's part being obedience. Archaeology finds Jericho's walls fell several times over the centuries; the text is less a war report than a liturgy of trust.

t: 'Choose this day whom you will serve'
n: Joshua's farewell at Sichem puts the choice starkly and answers for himself: 'as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord'. The covenant is renewed by free choice, not inheritance — the pattern every generation must repeat.

Gideon asks God for a sign twice — dew on the fleece and not the ground, then the reverse. God patiently obliges. Medieval readers saw the dew-soaked fleece as the Virgin Mary receiving the Word 'as rain upon the fleece' (Ps 71:6 in the Vulgate).

The strongest man in Israel is undone by nagging: 'she pressed him much... his soul fainted away'. Samson's story is the tragedy of gifts without discipline, and yet Hebrews 11 names him among the heroes of faith. His death, killing more in his death than in his life, was read as a shadow of the cross.

A Moabite widow refuses to leave her Israelite mother-in-law: 'whithersoever thou shalt go, I will go... thy God my God'. Ruth, a foreigner, becomes the great-grandmother of David and stands in Jesus' family tree — the book's quiet argument that God's people is entered by loyalty, not birth.

The boy Samuel hears his name three times in the night and thinks it is the old priest calling. Eli, whose own sons are corrupt, teaches him the answer. 'The word of the Lord was precious in those days' — rare — and it comes to a child.

'Give us a king to judge us, as all nations have.' God takes it personally — 'they have not rejected thee, but me' — yet grants it, after Samuel lists what kings do: conscript your sons, tax your fields, take your daughters. The monarchy begins under a shadow it never entirely escapes.

t: 'Man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart'
n: Samuel is ready to anoint the tall eldest son; God chooses the youngest, out with the sheep. David's anointing sets the pattern for the Messiah ('anointed one'). The verse became a proverb in every language the Bible touched.

The shepherd refuses Saul's armour and takes five smooth stones. His speech before the fight — 'thou comest to me with a sword... but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts' — is the point of the story. It has served as the emblem of every small cause facing a giant since.

David wants to build God a house (a temple); God answers that he will build David a house (a dynasty): 'thy throne shall be firm for ever'. This oracle is the root of all messianic hope — Gabriel quotes it to Mary (Luke 1:32–33). When the dynasty fell in 586 BC, the promise had to be understood on a larger scale.

After David has taken Bethsabee and had her husband killed, the prophet Nathan tells him a story about a rich man who steals a poor man's one lamb. David explodes in anger — and Nathan turns it on him. David's two words of reply, 'I have sinned', are the seed of Psalm 50 (51), the Miserere.

Two women, one living child, and an order to cut it in half. The real mother gives the baby up rather than see him die. The story shows wisdom as insight into the human heart, not cleverness — and it made 'a judgment of Solomon' a phrase in every European language.

'How long do you halt between two sides?' Elias (Elijah) sets one altar against four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, mocks their god ('perhaps he is asleep'), drenches his own sacrifice in water, and fire falls. It is the great showdown of the Old Testament; Carmelite monks still trace their origin to this mountain.

Fleeing for his life, Elias meets God on Horeb — not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in 'a whistling of a gentle air' (sibilus auræ tenuis). The God of Sinai's thunder now speaks in a whisper. It is one of the Bible's quietest and most quoted moments.

t: Elias taken up in a chariot of fire
n: Because Elias did not die, Israel expected him to return before the Messiah (Mal 4:5); a chair is still left for him at Passover. Jesus says John the Baptist was the Elias who was to come (Matt 11:14). Eliseus' request for a 'double portion' is the share of a firstborn heir.

A Syrian general expects a grand ritual and is told to bathe in a muddy river. His servants' logic — 'if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing...' — persuades him. Jesus cites Naaman as proof that God's grace reaches beyond Israel (Luke 4:27), and the Fathers saw baptism in the seven dips.

Nabuchodonosor's general burns the Temple, breaks down the walls and deports the people to Babylon. Everything the story had built since Abraham — land, king, temple — is gone in one chapter. Out of this catastrophe come Lamentations, Ezechiel, the second half of Isaiah, and a faith that could survive without a temple.
